extracted.subtask_description: Practical classroom assessment methods for undergraduate mathematics courses, including design and scoring guidance for short writing assignments (true/false with explanation, define/compare, student-created problems), resume/self-introduction tasks, and in-depth interviews to probe understanding.

rubrics_metrics.name: Resume / self-introduction assignment requirements
rubrics_metrics.description: Write a 2-page self-introduction to a potential employer presenting student activities (including mathematics classes) as evidence for potential as an employee.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide examples of former student letters and instructor recommendation letters (names erased) to model tone and content; emphasize connecting class work and projects to future job prospects; allow reworkings if responses are trivial; instructor may select exceptional student work to append to recommendation letters.

rubrics_metrics.name: Design of true/false statements
rubrics_metrics.description: Statements are designed to test understanding of specific theoretical points including definitions, properties, theorems, and relations among concepts, often cast in the form of implications.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Critical step is to identify aspects that are (i) most important and (ii) most likely to be misunderstood; purpose is not to trip students on subtle technicalities but to call attention to critical features (e.g., hypothesis vs conclusion, contrapositives, converse).

rubrics_metrics.name: True/false: explanation audience requirement
rubrics_metrics.description: Students must give a complete written argument addressed to a fellow student whom they are trying to convince of their reply.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Framing the audience as a peer encourages convincing, logical arguments consistent with students' level; in upper-division courses more formalism/rigor is expected.

rubrics_metrics.name: True/false: use of diagrams, examples, counterexamples
rubrics_metrics.description: Students should use diagrams, examples, or counterexamples as appropriate to supplement their written responses.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Counterexamples are especially valuable for false statements; brief, focused explanations are acceptable since questions target a specific concept.

rubrics_metrics.name: Administration timing and collaboration for true/false assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: Students are typically allowed three to five days to complete the assignment and are encouraged to discuss the questions with each other and with the instructor during this time.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students who wish to discuss the assignments with the instructor must show significant prior attempt; including these assignments frequently (e.g., weekly) helps students become familiar with format and expectations.

rubrics_metrics.name: Scoring emphasis for true/false tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Credit is given primarily for the explanations rather than the true/false response; composition and content are considered with emphasis on content.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A weak explanation for a correct response may earn less credit than a good explanation for a wrong response; in-class or exam versions should allocate extra time to allow for written explanations.

rubrics_metrics.name: True/false scoring procedure and rubrics
rubrics_metrics.description: Use a simple analytic/holistic scale (three- or five-point) and a generic scoring guide shared with students; read responses twice: once to comment and sort into rough piles, a second time to verify consistency and assign a score.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tailor the generic scoring guide to specific assignments by setting concrete content benchmarks for each score; examples of such scales are referenced (Emenaker).

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructional uses of true/false writing assignments
rubrics_metrics.description: Use student responses to identify misconceptions and modify instruction; use statements to prompt students to discover exceptional cases themselves rather than having the instructor present them.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Responses can reveal conceptual confusions (e.g., role of derivatives in extrema) and indicate needs for curricular changes (e.g., exploring universal vs existential quantification).

rubrics_metrics.name: Success scaffolding for true/false tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: Expect initially poor responses that improve after students become familiar with the format; provide specific written comments and encourage revisions or reworkings.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Share samples of strong/medium/weak student responses with the class, show transparencies for discussion, and offer alternatives (oral interview/transcription) for students for whom writing is a barrier (non-native speakers, learning-disabled).

rubrics_metrics.name: Define/Compare/Contrast assignment structure
rubrics_metrics.description: Hand out 10–12 short questions one week before a test requiring students to explain, describe, compare, contrast, or define mathematical concepts or terms using correct mathematical language.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: These serve as a review and force precision in mathematical language; expect correct terminology and whole-sentence explanations; warn students the tasks require more than routine problem solving.

rubrics_metrics.name: Verbal and graphical expectations for conceptual explanations
rubrics_metrics.description: Full credit often requires both verbal explanation and appropriate visual representation (e.g., graphs or geometric transformations) to illustrate differences or identities.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Example: To explain why sin(2x) ≠ 2 sin x students must describe horizontal compression vs vertical stretch, state effects on period and range, and sketch both graphs.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grading emphasis for definition/compare tasks
rubrics_metrics.description: When grading, instructors point out grammar and spelling errors but do not heavily penalize them; primary interest is in students' mathematical understanding.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Provide extensive comments to deepen understanding; avoid simply marking answers incorrect; discuss common errors with class when multiple students make the same mistake.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student-created problems: assignment structure
rubrics_metrics.description: For each major unit, each student constructs a word problem and its solution relevant to the unit's concepts; problems are collected, organized, checked for accuracy, and can be used as study guides.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Students may work individually or in small groups; provide several days to draft and submit; allow discussion and instructor advisement during development.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student-created problems: grading criteria
rubrics_metrics.description: Problems are graded on the basis of correctness, relevance to the topic, and originality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: If a student corrects and resubmits a problem, the corrected version receives the full value as if submitted correctly initially; provide examples of problems in each grading category to guide students.

rubrics_metrics.name: Student-created problems: integration and weight
rubrics_metrics.description: Use the collection of student problems as test material, study guides, or final-exam items; the collection can be assigned a significant course weight (e.g., one test = 25% of final grade).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Organize and edit the set for class distribution; using student problems on tests reduces complaints and increases perceived fairness.

rubrics_metrics.name: Operational policies for student-created problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Establish clear administrative rules: give ample time, adopt a no-late-submissions policy, require relevance to assigned topics, and return graded work promptly for revision and reuse.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Demonstrate expected problems, involve students in grading discussions, encourage electronic submission when possible to simplify compiling and distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Instructor workload considerations for student-created problems
rubrics_metrics.description: Reading, solving, and grading student-created problems is time-consuming—possibly three times longer than grading routine tests—because each submission is unique.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Balance the higher grading cost against saved time from not constructing tests and increased student engagement; limit late work to avoid end-of-term overload.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use of student work portfolios
rubrics_metrics.description: Keep portfolios of selected strong/medium/weak student responses to represent the range of class responses and to mine for evidence of teaching effectiveness and student learning.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Portfolios provide a resource for reflection, future class examples, and supplemental material for recommendation letters; review portfolios periodically to adjust instruction.

rubrics_metrics.name: In-depth interviews: non-evaluative probing
rubrics_metrics.description: Use content-based interviews to probe students' mathematical understanding with the stated goal of understanding how students think rather than assigning grades.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Tell students the interview's purpose to encourage candid responses; use follow-up probing to reveal depth (or lack) of conceptual understanding that test answers may obscure; interviews can inform teaching improvement.
